title: The fire made cool
hookLine: they throw Ibrahim into a great fire and Allah says, fire, be cool and safe for him (21:68–69)

cards: A crowd embarrassed in front of itself doesn't always change its mind. Sometimes it gets angry. This week has been full of people who paid for speaking up.
Nuh, calling for nine hundred and fifty years, building a ship on dry land while people laughed, calling to his son as the wave came between them.
Ibrahim, watching the star set, breaking the idols, letting the town hear itself say: they cannot speak. Nuh was mocked. Ibrahim is about to find out what it costs.

teach.h: BURN HIM, AND STAND BY YOUR GODS.
teach.b: Surah twenty-one. The crowd has lost the argument, so they reach for the only thing left. In Pickthall's words: “Burn him and stand by your gods, if ye will be doing.”
The commentators' retellings make the fire enormous: wood gathered for days, a blaze so hot that birds flying over it fell, Ibrahim thrown in from a distance by a kind of catapult.
Those details are tradition; the Qur'an doesn't give them.

teach.h: O FIRE, BE COOL AND SAFE.
teach.b: What it gives is one sentence, God speaking to the fire itself: “O fire, be coolness and peace for Abraham.” In Arabic, bardan wa salaman.
Cool, and safe. And the fire obeys. The commentators preserve an old observation: if God had said only be cool, the fire might have frozen him.
So He said cool, and safe.
Exactly enough. What was Ibrahim doing as he fell? A report in Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, says his words were: hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil.
God is enough for us, and the best one to trust. The same words, the report says, were later said by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions when they were told an army was gathering against them.
The line is still said today in moments of fear. Notice the order. Ibrahim didn't wait to see whether the fire would cool before he trusted.
The trust came first, in midair.
The coolness came after. And the verse doesn't say the fire went out. It says what the fire was told to be.

how: Many Muslims say hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil, God is enough for us and the best one to trust, in moments of fear, remembering Ibrahim in the fire.

games.q: what does “the fire made cool” mean?
o: rain fell and put out the flames around him
God told the fire to be cool and safe for him
Ibrahim walked out before the flames rose

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: burn him, and stand by your gods

s: the Qur'an describes birds falling from the heat of the fire
that comes from the commentators' retellings. the Qur'an gives one sentence to the fire.
God told the fire to be cool and also safe
"O fire, be coolness and peace for Abraham."
a report says Ibrahim's words in the fire were: God is enough for us
hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil (Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas).

games.q: you're Ibrahim, thrown toward a fire so big nobody can get near it. what do you say as you fall?
o: save me, and I'll do anything.
God is enough for us, and the best one to trust.
games.why: the report in Bukhari says: hasbuna llahu wa ni'ma l-wakil. the trust came first. then God said: O fire, be cool and safe.

practice: Think of something that feels like a fire right now, a deadline, a conflict, a fear burning in the background, and feel its heat for a moment.
Then breathe out slowly, all the way, three times, long cool breaths like wind across the flames, and rest. If you pray, you can hold Ibrahim's words: God is enough for us.

wordCard.voice: The fire made cool. Bardan wa salaman: God tells the fire to be cool and safe for Ibrahim, and it is.

orig.note: Arabic: "coolness and peace," what God tells the fire to be for Ibrahim (21:69).

carryVoice: Your line: cool and safe. Two words from God, and the fire listened. Five weeks, done.
